debug.title: A password form that puts the value in the URL
debug.broken:
<form action="/login" method="get">
  <label for="password">Password</label>
  <input id="password" name="password" type="password">
  <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>
debug.fix:
<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="password">Password</label>
  <input id="password" name="password" type="password">
  <button type="submit">Sign in</button>
</form>
debug.error: GET submits the password in the query string, where it lands in history, logs and referrers. Credentials belong in a POST body.

debug.title: A reset button that submits instead
debug.error: Missing type: a button inside a form defaults to submit, so the control labelled Reset saves the form instead of clearing it.

interview.q: GET or POST for a login form, and why?
interview.answer: POST. GET puts the credentials in the URL, which is stored in history, server logs and referrer headers, and it can be triggered by a link or prefetch.

interview.q: Why must every input have a name?
interview.answer: The name is the key in the submitted form data. Without it the control is omitted from the submission entirely, no matter what the user typed.

interview.q: What actually happens when a form submits?
interview.answer: The browser validates the controls, builds a form data set from the successful controls, encodes it according to the method and enctype, sends the request to the action URL and navigates to the response.

debug.title: An impossible number range
debug.broken:
<label for="age">Age</label>
<input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="18" max="10">
debug.fix:
<label for="age">Age</label>
<input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="10" max="18">

debug.title: Checkboxes that never submit
debug.error: Missing name and value: an unnamed control is never included in the form data, so the server cannot tell whether it was ticked.

interview.q: Client-side validation versus server-side — what do you tell a junior?
interview.answer: Client-side validation is a convenience for the user; server-side validation is the security boundary. The client can be bypassed by disabling scripts, editing the DOM or sending a direct request.

interview.q: readonly or disabled — which one?
interview.answer: readonly keeps the value visible and submitted but not editable. disabled removes it from submission, from the tab order and usually from the accessibility tree.

interview.q: How do you add a pattern without making errors unusable?
interview.answer: Keep the pattern simple and documented next to the field, give a concrete example, keep the label visible, and never rely on the pattern alone: validate again on the server and return a specific message.

debug.title: A caption track with no language
debug.error: Missing srclang: a caption track needs a language, and the browser may refuse to offer it in the caption menu.

debug.title: Audio that autoplays with sound
debug.error: Audible autoplay is blocked by most browsers, so the media never starts; the supported pattern is muted autoplay with a visible control.

interview.q: What is the difference between captions and subtitles?
interview.answer: Captions transcribe dialogue and meaningful sounds for viewers who cannot hear the audio. Subtitles translate dialogue for viewers who can hear it but do not understand the language.

interview.q: mp4 or webm — how do you choose?
interview.answer: Offer both with source elements: mp4 with H.264 has the widest device support, webm often compresses better. The browser picks the first type it can play.

interview.q: Why do browsers restrict autoplay?
interview.answer: Unexpected sound is hostile to users and costly on mobile data, so browsers require a user gesture for audible playback. Muted autoplay and playsinline are the supported exceptions.

debug.title: Two title elements
debug.error: Duplicate title: the parser keeps the first and drops the rest, so the intended title never appears.

debug.title: Noindex left on a public page
debug.error: Staging directive shipped to production: search engines are told to drop the page, which can take weeks to reverse.

interview.q: What problem does the canonical link solve?
interview.answer: It names the preferred URL when the same content is reachable at several addresses, so ranking signals consolidate on one page instead of being split.

interview.q: How do you audit a page’s metadata?
interview.answer: Check one title, one description, one canonical, the Open Graph set and the favicon in the head; verify with link preview tools and a crawler view, not just the source.

interview.q: noindex or a robots.txt disallow — what is the difference?
interview.answer: noindex is a per-page directive that lets a crawler fetch the page and then drop it from results. Disallow blocks fetching, so a noindex inside a disallowed page is never seen.

debug.title: A link pretending to be a button

debug.title: A meaningful image hidden from assistive technology
debug.error: aria-hidden on a content image removes it from the accessibility tree, so the information it carries is lost to screen-reader users.
debug.fixedOutput: Marks rose from 60 to 90 across three terms (image)

interview.q: What is the accessibility tree?
interview.answer: The browser’s representation of the page for assistive technology: roles, names, states and relationships derived from the DOM, CSS and ARIA. It is what a screen reader actually navigates.

interview.q: When is ARIA necessary?
interview.answer: When no native element expresses the pattern, or when a native element needs an additional name, state or relationship. If a native element already provides the semantics, ARIA only adds risk.

interview.q: How do you test keyboard accessibility?
interview.answer: Unplug the mouse: tab through every control in a logical order, confirm a visible focus indicator, operate menus and dialogs with Enter, Space, Escape and arrows, and check that focus never disappears behind a layer.

debug.title: A sandbox that blocks the widget
debug.error: Empty sandbox: scripts, forms and popups are all blocked, so an interactive widget renders but does nothing.

debug.title: An insecure embed on an HTTPS page
debug.error: Mixed content: an http subresource on an https page is blocked by the browser, leaving an empty frame.

interview.q: What risks does an iframe introduce?
interview.answer: It loads a second document with its own scripts and network access, can attempt top navigation and popups, adds a request that can delay the page, and can capture keyboard focus inside content you do not control.

interview.q: What does a sandbox without allow-same-origin guarantee?
interview.answer: The framed document gets an opaque origin: it cannot read cookies or storage for its own origin and cannot reach the parent through same-origin access. Combined with allow-scripts it can still run its own code.

interview.q: When is an iframe the wrong tool?
interview.answer: For embedding your own page structure, for navigation, and for layout. If the content is yours, render it in the document; if it is a full independent page, a link is safer and faster.

interview.q: dialog or a custom modal div?
interview.answer: dialog gives focus management, Escape handling, a backdrop and top-layer rendering natively. A div modal has to reimplement all of it and usually gets focus trapping wrong.

interview.q: progress or meter?
interview.answer: progress reports completion of a task and may be indeterminate. meter displays a measurement in a known range with low, high and optimum semantics.

interview.q: What is the template element for?
interview.answer: Holding inert markup that is not rendered or executed until a script clones it. It is the native way to keep reusable fragments in the document.

debug.title: defer on an inline script
debug.error: defer is ignored for inline scripts: the code runs immediately, before the button exists, so the lookup returns null.

debug.title: A stylesheet limited to print
debug.error: A print media attribute: the browser downloads the stylesheet but applies it only when printing, so the screen stays unstyled.

interview.q: Where should script tags go, and why?
interview.answer: In the head with defer for most pages: download starts early, execution waits for parsing and keeps document order. A classic script without defer blocks parsing and should sit at the end of body if it must.

interview.q: How do HTML and JavaScript communicate without tight coupling?
interview.answer: Through a small contract: ids for labels and fragments, data attributes for behaviour values, and events instead of inline handlers. The markup does not need to know how the script works.

interview.q: What happens if the stylesheet fails to load?
interview.answer: The HTML still renders in document order with the browser’s default styles. That is why structure and reading order must make sense without CSS, and why critical layout should not depend on a single remote file.

debug.title: A link wrapped around the wrong heading boundary
debug.error: Misnested tags: the parser closes the anchor before the heading ends, so the link may cover less than intended and the DOM differs from the source.

debug.title: An unescaped ampersand in a URL
debug.error: Raw ampersand: validators read it as the start of a character reference, and the query can be parsed incorrectly.

interview.q: How do you debug a page that renders differently from its source?
interview.answer: Compare the Elements panel with the original response: the parser repairs invalid nesting, and scripts may have changed the tree. The first difference points at the markup that caused it.

interview.q: What does the W3C validator not catch?
interview.answer: Accessibility quality, whether the heading order matches the content, misleading alt text, vague link text, visual design and performance. It checks conformance, not judgement.

interview.q: What is your pre-launch HTML checklist?
interview.answer: Valid markup, one h1 and a sane outline, lang and charset, unique title and description, alt text, labelled controls, working links, one main landmark, keyboard pass and no console errors.

interview.q: How do you plan a multi-page site?
interview.answer: Decide the pages and their purpose, the shared header, nav and footer, the folder structure for assets, and the URL scheme before writing markup. Every page then differs only inside main.

interview.q: What do you check before handing a site to a client?
interview.answer: Every page valid and linked, navigation consistent, forms reaching a real handler, alt text and labels present, metadata set, keyboard and mobile pass, and no console or 404 errors.

interview.q: How do you keep shared markup consistent without a framework?
interview.answer: Keep one reference page as the template, copy its header and footer verbatim, keep relative paths and labels identical, and validate after every change so drift is caught immediately.
